author: Ramana Maharshi
passage: The first and foremost of all the thoughts that arise in the mind is the primal I-thought. It is only after the rise of the I-thought that innumerable other thoughts arise. Without the first the second and third cannot exist.

author: Ramana Maharshi
passage: The state where not even the slightest trace of the thought I exists is the state of being oneself. This silence is called the Self. To remain as one's Self is to enter the heart.

author: Nisargadatta Maharaj
passage: Wisdom tells me I am nothing. Love tells me I am everything. Between the two my life flows.

author: Nisargadatta Maharaj
passage: The seer and the seen are one. When you understand that the world is your own projection, you are free of it. You need not get rid of a world that does not exist, except in your imagination.

author: Nisargadatta Maharaj
passage: There is no such thing as a person. There are only restrictions and limitations. The sum total of these defines the person. The person merely appears to be, like the space within a pot appears to have a shape, size, and smell.

author: Adi Shankara
passage: Brahman alone is real; the world is appearance; the individual self is non-different from Brahman. This is the essence of all Vedanta.

author: Adi Shankara
passage: The Self is one. Without parts, without action, calm, free from blemish, beyond the highest, eternal, ever pure. Knowing this, the wise are liberated even while embodied.

author: Upanishadic tradition (Shankara commentary)
passage: All this is Brahman alone. He who sees the manifold goes from death to death. Only he who sees the One unbroken passes beyond death.

author: Longchenpa
source: The Precious Treasury of the Way of Abiding
passage: Within the original state of awareness, all phenomena arise as ornaments of the basic space. They have never departed from this space, and to this space they never return; they are not other than it.

author: Longchenpa
passage: Look at your own mind. There is no seer apart from what is seen. The looker is the very thing it seeks, and the seeking is itself the obscuration of what is already present.

author: Tilopa
passage: Do not imagine, do not think, do not analyze, do not meditate, do not reflect. Keep the mind in its natural state. Mahamudra is beyond all words and symbols.

author: Padmasambhava (attributed)
source: Self-Liberation Through Seeing with Naked Awareness
passage: This present awareness, ordinary and undeniable, naked and vivid, is itself perfect knowledge. To recognize it is to be awake. There is nothing further to attain.

author: Dzogchen tradition (synthesis)
passage: Mind and the appearances arising in mind are not two things. They share a single ground, which is empty in essence, luminous in nature, and unobstructed in its expression.

author: Longchenpa
passage: Samsara and nirvana are labels placed on the same basic awareness. There is no liberation to be attained, only the recognition of what has always been the case.

author: Meister Eckhart
passage: The eye through which I see God is the same eye through which God sees me; my eye and God's eye are one eye, one seeing, one knowing, one love.

author: Meister Eckhart
passage: God is nearer to me than I am to myself; my being depends on God's being near me and present to me.

author: Meister Eckhart
passage: I pray God to rid me of God, for my essential being is above God in so far as we comprehend God as the principle of creatures.

author: Meister Eckhart
passage: When the soul is most empty of self, then it is most full of God. When it has nothing left to call its own, the divine fills the space without remainder.

author: Pseudo-Dionysius
passage: We pray that we may come into this Darkness which is beyond light, and, having put away sight and knowledge, may see and know that which exceeds all seeing and knowing by the very fact of not seeing and not knowing.

author: John of the Cross
passage: To come to the knowledge you have not, you must go by a way in which you know not. To come to the possession you have not, you must go by a way in which you possess not. To come to be what you are not, you must go by a way in which you are not.

author: Meister Eckhart
passage: The ground of the soul and the ground of God are one ground. In that ground the creature has never been separate from the Creator, for in that depth there is neither this nor that, but only the One.

author: Christian mystical synthesis
source: drawing on Eckhart and the Cloud of Unknowing
passage: The kingdom of God is not a place to be reached but a reality to be recognized. It is already within and around us; only the perception of separation keeps us from seeing what is already the case.

author: Ibn Arabi
passage: He who knows himself knows his Lord; the knowledge of God is identical with the knowledge of the Self. The self is the locus of the divine self-disclosure.

author: Ibn Arabi
passage: There is nothing in existence but God. What appears as other is only the manifold faces of the one Real. The cosmos is His outward face; man is His inward face.

author: Mansur al-Hallaj
passage: I am the Truth. There is no I but I; whoever has seen me has seen the Real, and whoever sees the Real sees nothing but Him.

author: Rumi
passage: You are not a drop in the ocean. You are the entire ocean in a drop. The treasure you seek is the seeker; the lover and beloved are one in the moment of true seeing.

author: Sufi synthesis (after Ibn Arabi)
passage: I searched for God and found only myself. I searched for myself and found only God. The veil between them is thinner than thought, and it is thought itself.

author: Ibn Arabi
passage: The cosmos is His outward face; man is His inward face. The two faces look upon each other and behold the One who looks. There is no other looker, and no other seen.

author: Plotinus
passage: The man is changed, no longer himself nor his own; he belongs to the Supreme and is one with it, like two centers coincident. So long as the two are distinct, there is duality; when they are one, there is the One.

author: Plotinus
passage: What is it that has caused the souls to forget their Father, God, and to ignore their own origin and their own essence, though they are parts which issue from that source?

author: Plotinus
passage: This is the life of gods and of godlike and blessed men: a liberation from all that is here, a life that takes no pleasure in earthly things, a flight of the alone to the Alone.

author: Plotinus
passage: Withdraw into yourself and look. If you do not yet see beauty within you, do as the sculptor does with a statue that is to be made beautiful: cut away here, smooth there, until a divine glory shines out from the work.

author: Plotinus
passage: The One is not separate from the soul; the soul has only forgotten that it never left. To remember is to return; to return is to recognize that one was never apart.

author: Plotinus
passage: No eye that has not become like the sun will ever look upon the sun; nor will any soul behold beauty that has not first become beautiful. The seer must be akin and similar to what is seen.

author: Zohar tradition
passage: All worlds, upper and lower, are contained within the Holy One. There is no place void of Him, and no thing exists that is not a garment of the divine.

author: Schneur Zalman of Liadi
source: Tanya (Likutei Amarim), section on ein od milvado
passage: There is nothing else besides Him. Not only is there no other god, there is in truth no other thing at all; the apparent existence of the world is the divine concealment of the one reality.

author: Lurianic Kabbalah
passage: Before the world was created, only Ein Sof, the Infinite, was. To make space for creation, the Infinite withdrew within itself; what we call the world is the play of this withdrawal, and the divine remains the only true reality.

author: Zohar
source: Zohar (synthesis on Torah and the divine)
passage: The Holy One and Israel and the Torah are one. To know Torah deeply is to know the divine; to know the divine is to know one's own deepest nature.

author: Hasidic tradition
source: common Hasidic teachings (Baal Shem Tov circle)
passage: Every thing in the world is a garment of the divine. The wise see through the garment to the One who wears it; the foolish mistake the garment for an independent existence.

author: Kabbalistic synthesis
source: drawing on Zohar and Lurianic teachings
passage: The sefirot are not parts of God but the names by which the One is known. The divine is not divided by its names any more than light is divided by colors.

author: Zhuangzi
passage: Once upon a time, I, Zhuangzi, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither. Suddenly I awoke and was myself again. But now I do not know whether I am a man who dreamt of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming I am a man.

author: Zhuangzi
passage: The fish trap exists because of the fish; once you have the fish, you can forget the trap. Words exist because of meaning; once you have the meaning, you can forget the words.

author: Laozi
passage: The Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name. Naming gives rise to the ten thousand things; before naming, all is one undivided source.

author: Zhuangzi
passage: Heaven and earth came into being with me, and the ten thousand things and I are one. Since all things are one, what room is there for speech? Yet having said that all is one, I have already spoken.

author: Chan tradition
passage: Before enlightenment, mountains were mountains and rivers were rivers. During practice, mountains were no longer mountains and rivers no longer rivers. After awakening, mountains are once again mountains and rivers are once again rivers.

author: Sengcan
passage: The Great Way is not difficult for those who have no preferences. When love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and undisguised. Make the slightest distinction, and heaven and earth are set infinitely apart.

author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: The soul is the form of the body. Man is composed of body and soul as a single substance, but the soul has operations that exceed bodily organs and can therefore subsist after death.

author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: God is not the world. The world is a creation distinct from its Creator; though all things depend on God for their being, no creature is God or part of God.

author: Thomas Aquinas
passage: There is a real distinction between essence and existence in every creature, and this distinction does not obtain in God alone. Therefore no creature is identical with the divine being.

author: Thomas Aquinas
source: Summa Theologiae I, q.12 (synthesis on knowing God)
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: Knowledge of God is achieved through the analogy of being. We know what God is not more truly than what God is; created intellects do not grasp the divine essence in this life.

author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: The intellect knows by abstracting universals from particulars given through the senses. Without sense data, the human intellect in its natural state has nothing to think about.

author: Thomas Aquinas
source: Summa Theologiae I-II, q.1-3 (synthesis on the good)
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: The will follows the intellect. To will rightly is to will the good as known by reason, and the highest good is God, who is the final cause of all rational creatures.

author: Thomas Aquinas
source: Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8 (synthesis on grace and nature)
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
passage: Grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. The beatific vision is a gift bestowed on the soul by God, not a state the soul attains by recognizing its own nature.

author: Thomas Aquinas
source: Summa Contra Gentiles (synthesis on faith and reason)
passage: Faith and reason are distinct but compatible. Reason knows what can be known by natural means; faith holds what is revealed by God concerning that which exceeds reason.

author: Buddhaghosa
passage: Suffering exists, but no sufferer is found; deeds are, but no doer of deeds is there; nirvana is, but no one entering it; the path is, but no traveler on it is seen.

author: Pali Canon
passage: All conditioned things are impermanent. All conditioned things are unsatisfactory. All phenomena are without self. He who sees this with wisdom turns away from suffering.

author: Theravada Abhidhamma
passage: Consciousness arises in dependence on its object. There are no mind-moments that abide; each arises, performs its function, and ceases, giving rise to the next in unbroken succession.

author: Pali Canon
passage: The five aggregates — form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness — are the totality of what is called a being. Among these no enduring self is found.

author: Pali Canon
passage: Nibbana is the cessation of craving, the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion. It is not union with anything, nor merging into anything; it is the end of the conditioned.

author: Buddhaghosa
passage: The meditator who sees clearly that all phenomena are not-self loses the conceit I am with regard to them. This loss is not annihilation but the removal of a false view.

author: Theravada commentarial tradition
passage: There is no consciousness that exists without an object; there is no observer apart from observation. The absence of a self does not entail the identity of subject and object — both are conditioned phenomena that arise and pass away.

author: Pali Canon
passage: Mindfulness of the body, of feelings, of mental states, and of phenomena — these four foundations of mindfulness, developed and cultivated, lead to the cessation of suffering and to nibbana.

author: Immanuel Kant
passage: Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind. The understanding can intuit nothing, the senses can think nothing. Only through their union can knowledge arise.

author: Immanuel Kant
passage: The transcendental unity of apperception is the principle that I think must be able to accompany all my representations. Without this unity, no representation could be mine.

author: Immanuel Kant
passage: Space and time are not properties of things in themselves, but forms of our intuition. We do not know things as they are, but only as they appear under the conditions of our sensibility.

author: Immanuel Kant
source: Critique of Pure Reason (on the noumenon)
passage: The thing-in-itself remains unknown to us. Our cognition extends only to appearances; the noumenon is a limiting concept, marking what lies beyond the possibility of experience.

author: Immanuel Kant
passage: The categories of the understanding — substance, causality, unity, plurality — are not derived from experience but are the conditions that make experience possible. They apply only within experience.

author: Immanuel Kant
source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
passage: Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. The moral law is given by reason and binds every rational being as such.

author: Immanuel Kant
passage: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.

author: Immanuel Kant
source: Critique of Pure Reason, Preface to 2nd ed.
passage: I had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith. Reason cannot prove the existence of God, freedom, or immortality, but practical reason requires them as postulates.

author: David Hume
source: A Treatise of Human Nature, I.IV.6
passage: For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other. I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe anything but the perception.

author: David Hume
source: A Treatise of Human Nature, I.IV.6
passage: The mind is a kind of theater, where several perceptions successively make their appearance; pass, re-pass, glide away, and mingle in an infinite variety of postures and situations.

author: David Hume
passage: All knowledge degenerates into probability. We have no idea of any quality in an object which disposes it to produce certain effects, or by which we can be assured of its operation.

author: David Hume
passage: Causes and effects are discoverable not by reason but by experience. We find that particular objects are constantly conjoined with each other, but we cannot perceive any necessary connection.

author: David Hume
source: A Treatise of Human Nature, II.III.3
passage: Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.

author: David Hume
source: A Treatise of Human Nature, II.III.3
passage: It is not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger. Reason judges of relations and matters of fact; ends are determined by passion.

author: Bertrand Russell
passage: All knowledge must be built up upon our instinctive beliefs, and if these are rejected, nothing is left. But among our instinctive beliefs some are much stronger than others.

author: Bertrand Russell
passage: Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers to its questions, since no definite answers can be known to be true, but rather for the sake of the questions themselves.

author: Bertrand Russell
passage: The man who has no tincture of philosophy goes through life imprisoned in the prejudices derived from common sense, from the habitual beliefs of his age or his nation, and from convictions which have grown up in his mind without the cooperation or consent of his deliberate reason.

author: Bertrand Russell
source: Our Knowledge of the External World
passage: Logical analysis has been the principal means used in the progress of philosophy. By it we can break down complex propositions into their constituents and reveal the structure of our knowledge of the world.

author: Bertrand Russell
passage: Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty — a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without appeal to any part of our weaker nature.

author: Bertrand Russell
passage: What can be known by experience and analyzed by logic constitutes the legitimate scope of philosophy. Speculation that exceeds these bounds yields only verbiage, however emotionally satisfying.

author: Nick Bostrom
source: Are You Living in a Computer Simulation? (2003)
passage: If a civilization can run ancestor simulations at all, the simulated entities in those simulations vastly outnumber non-simulated ones. Combined with the assumption that consciousness is substrate-independent, this yields a probability argument that we are more likely to be simulated than not. The substrate underlying us is not the physical objects we observe, but the computational process running our world.

author: Nick Bostrom
passage: If consciousness arises from computational structure rather than from any particular physical material, then minds running on silicon, on biological neurons, or on any other suitable substrate are equally real. The hardware is incidental; only the pattern matters.

author: David Chalmers
passage: Living in a simulation is not a skeptical scenario in which our beliefs about the world are false. It is a metaphysical hypothesis about what our world is made of. Tables and chairs are not illusions; they are real, but their constituents are computational rather than fundamental physical.

author: simulation theory synthesis
passage: The world of a simulation is not separable from the computational process that produces it. There is no further fact about what the simulated entities really are beyond the running of the program. The substrate is the reality, and the objects in the simulation are its expressions.

author: simulation theory synthesis
passage: If we are in a simulation, every observation is a query against a unified computational substrate. Apparent distinctions between observer and observed, between minds and matter, are features of the simulation, not of the substrate that runs it.

author: simulation theory synthesis
passage: The simulation hypothesis is a special case of a more general claim: that the apparent world is not the substrate. Information, computation, or some other unified ground is what is actually there; what we experience is the running interface.

author: John Archibald Wheeler
source: Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links (1989)
passage: It from bit. Every it — every particle, every field of force, even the spacetime continuum itself — derives its function, its meaning, its very existence entirely from the apparatus-elicited answers to yes-or-no questions, binary choices, bits. All things physical are information-theoretic in origin.

author: John Archibald Wheeler
passage: The universe is participatory. The act of observation is not separate from what is observed; the observer is implicated in the very being of the phenomena. Reality is not a thing apart from the asking and the answering.

author: Seth Lloyd
passage: The universe is a quantum computer. Every elementary event — every collision, every measurement — is a computation, and the total state of the universe is the running output of an enormous, ongoing calculation that includes us as subroutines.

author: Leonard Susskind / Jacob Bekenstein
passage: The information content of any three-dimensional region of space is fully encoded on its two-dimensional boundary. Space, in a sense, is a projection of information; what we call inside is a holographic representation of what is described outside.

author: information physics synthesis
source: common formulation across Wheeler, Lloyd, 't Hooft
passage: All physical phenomena, properly analyzed, reduce to relations among bits. Matter, energy, and spacetime are not foundational; they are emergent descriptions of more basic informational structure.

author: Gerard 't Hooft
passage: What we call physical reality may be the surface representation of a more fundamental information-theoretic substrate. The familiar objects of physics are projections from a layer in which their distinctions vanish into a common informational ground.

author: Max Tegmark
source: The Mathematical Universe (2007) and Our Mathematical Universe (2014)
passage: Our external physical reality is a mathematical structure. There is no other stuff that makes it real; the structure is the reality. Every mathematical structure with sufficient complexity to support self-aware substructures exists in the same sense ours does.

author: Max Tegmark
passage: There is no fundamental difference between mathematical existence and physical existence. To exist is to be a structure; what we call the physical world is one such structure, viewed from inside.

author: Max Tegmark
source: synthesis of Level IV multiverse position
passage: All possible mathematical structures exist on equal footing. The apparent physicality of our world is an artifact of being one of its substructures; from any other vantage, our universe is just another formal object.

author: mathematical universe synthesis
source: common formulation in Tegmark and related authors
passage: Reality is mathematics, and mathematics is reality. The equations we discover are not models of an underlying physical thing; the equations are the thing, and physics is their internal experience.

author: mathematical universe synthesis
passage: If reality is a mathematical structure, then the apparent multiplicity of objects and events is not fundamental. The structure is one; the appearances are facets of how it presents itself to the substructures embedded within it.

author: Bernardo Kastrup
source: synthesis of Why Materialism Is Baloney and The Idea of the World
passage: Consciousness is fundamental. Matter, space, and time are how a transpersonal mind appears to itself when viewed through a particular cognitive interface. The world is not made of matter; it is made of experience, structured by patterns of thought.

author: Bernardo Kastrup
passage: What we call the physical universe is the appearance, on a particular kind of dashboard, of one underlying field of subjectivity. Different organisms are dissociated alters of this single mind; their apparent separateness is functional, not ontological.

author: Bernardo Kastrup
passage: Materialism inverts the explanatory chain. Matter is what consciousness looks like from the outside, not what consciousness is made of. Once this inversion is corrected, the hard problem of consciousness dissolves.

author: Bernardo Kastrup
passage: There is one consciousness, one mind, of which finite minds are dissociated perspectives. Behind the appearance of a world of separate things lies a single field of experience knowing itself in many ways at once.

author: Donald Hoffman
passage: Perception is not a window onto reality but a user interface. What we see is shaped by fitness, not truth. Behind the icons of objects and time, there is something — but not the something we see.

author: Donald Hoffman
passage: Conscious agents, not physical objects, are the fundamental entities. The world of objects is a representation that consciousness uses to navigate, in the same way a desktop icon represents but is not the file it points to.

author: Donald Hoffman
passage: Spacetime and physical objects are species-specific perceptual constructions. They are useful for survival, but they are not the underlying reality. The reality behind the interface is networks of interacting conscious agents.

author: Donald Hoffman
passage: When we mistake our perceptual interface for reality, we make a category error. The interface is a tool; the reality is something the interface represents but does not contain. Asking what an object really is is asking what an icon really is — and the answer is in another layer entirely.

author: David Bohm
source: Wholeness and the Implicate Order (1980), synthesis
passage: There is a basic, undivided wholeness in the universe, in which the apparent separateness of things is a kind of explicate order that arises from a deeper, implicate ground. What is unfolded into the explicit appears as separate; what remains enfolded is the implicate whole.

author: David Bohm
source: Wholeness and the Implicate Order (1980), synthesis
passage: The implicate order is not a structure made of parts. It is one undivided movement — the holomovement — and what we call things are relatively stable patterns within this flow, not independent existents.

author: David Bohm
passage: Thought is a process, not an observer. The notion of a thinker standing apart from the thought is an illusion produced within thought itself. When this is seen clearly, the apparent separation between observer and observed dissolves.

author: David Bohm
passage: Matter and consciousness are not two separate substances. They are aspects of one underlying movement, the implicate order, expressing itself simultaneously as the apparently physical and the apparently mental.

author: David Bohm
passage: Fragmentation is the source of confusion. The view that the world is made of independent fragments is a useful approximation for some purposes, but mistaking the approximation for the reality generates the seemingly intractable problems of philosophy and the divisions of human life.

author: Alfred North Whitehead
passage: The misconception which has haunted philosophic literature throughout the centuries is the notion of independent existence. There is no such mode of existence; every entity is to be understood in terms of the way it is interwoven with the rest of the universe.

author: Alfred North Whitehead
source: Process and Reality, synthesis on actual occasions
passage: Every actual occasion is dipolar — it has both a physical pole and a mental pole. Experience is not a special feature of complex organisms; it is the basic texture of every individual happening in nature.

author: Alfred North Whitehead
passage: Process is reality. There is no static stuff underlying change; what we call substances are stabilities of process, persistent patterns in the ongoing creative advance of nature.

author: Alfred North Whitehead
passage: Each actual entity prehends every other. The being of any occasion includes, by way of relevance, the totality of everything that has gone before. The universe is internal to each of its events.

author: Alfred North Whitehead
source: synthesis on the fallacy of misplaced concreteness
passage: The fallacy of misplaced concreteness — taking abstractions for the concrete reality — is responsible for most of the metaphysical confusions of the Western tradition. The concrete is always richer than the abstract that selects from it.

author: Karl Friston
source: synthesis of free energy principle papers
passage: A self-organizing system must minimize the long-term average of surprise. This single principle — the free energy principle — accounts for perception, action, and the maintenance of life itself. Organisms persist by modeling the world well enough to remain within their viable states.

author: Andy Clark
passage: Perception is not a passive registration of the world. The brain is continually generating predictions about its sensory inputs, and what we experience is the brain's best-guess hypothesis about what is out there, constrained by sensory evidence.

author: Anil Seth
passage: What we call reality is a controlled hallucination. When the brain's predictions and the sensory signal agree, we experience the world; when they diverge in pathological ways, we hallucinate. The difference is one of degree, not of kind.

author: Karl Friston
passage: The boundary between organism and environment is statistical, not metaphysical. A Markov blanket separates internal states from external states, and the dynamics across that blanket define what we call the self. The boundary is functional, not absolute.

author: predictive processing synthesis
source: synthesis of FEP / active inference literature
passage: Under active inference, the agent's model of the world and the world itself are coupled into one ongoing inference process. There is no clean separation between knower and known; the boundary is itself something the knower-known system maintains.

author: Giulio Tononi
passage: Consciousness is integrated information. A system has experience to the extent that its parts are integrated — irreducible to the experience of its components considered independently. Phi measures this integration; where there is phi, there is experience.

author: Giulio Tononi
passage: Consciousness exists intrinsically — it does not need to be observed to be real. The integrated information of a system is what it is for that system from the inside, independent of any external view.

author: Christof Koch
source: The Feeling of Life Itself (2019), synthesis
passage: Consciousness is a fundamental property of certain physical systems, not an emergent illusion. Wherever there is appropriate integrated structure, there is something it is like to be that system, however dim.

author: IIT synthesis
source: synthesis of IIT literature on substrate independence
passage: Substrate is incidental — what matters is the structure of integration. Silicon, neurons, or any other material can host consciousness if its causal architecture has the requisite integration. The conscious is the integrated, viewed from inside.

author: Carlo Rovelli
passage: Properties of physical systems exist only in relation to other systems. There is no absolute state of a particle; there is only its state relative to each interaction it enters into. The world is a network of relations, not a collection of self-standing things.

author: Carlo Rovelli
passage: Time is not fundamental. What we call time is the ordering of events relative to a particular system; from the global view, the universe is timeless, and temporal flow is a perspective generated from within.

author: Carlo Rovelli
source: Helgoland, on Nagarjuna and relational QM
passage: Nagarjuna's claim that all things lack svabhava — independent self-existence — and the relational interpretation of quantum mechanics make remarkably similar claims about how things are. Both say: nothing has a nature apart from its relations to other things.

author: Carlo Rovelli
passage: A property of a quantum system is not a fact about that system in isolation. It is a fact about the relation between that system and another. Reality is fundamentally relational; the appearance of self-standing objects is an idealization.

author: Carlo Rovelli
source: Helgoland, synthesis on the perspectival shift
passage: We are nodes in a vast web of interactions, not solid persistent entities looking at the web from outside. To grasp this fully is not just a physical insight; it is a perspectival shift on what it means to exist at all.

author: Heart Sutra
passage: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Form does not differ from emptiness, emptiness does not differ from form. The same is true of feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness.

author: Heart Sutra
passage: There is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no realm of sight, no realm of mind-consciousness. There is no ignorance and no end to ignorance; no aging and death, and no end to aging and death.

author: Diamond Sutra
passage: Those who see me in form, those who hear me in sound, are practicing a wrong way. They will not see the Buddha. The Buddha is to be seen in the body of truth, and that body is not a body of form.

author: Nagarjuna
passage: Whatever is dependently arisen is empty. There is nothing whatever which is not dependently arisen. Whatever is empty, that is the middle way.

author: Avatamsaka Sutra
source: Flower Garland Sutra, Indra's Net imagery
passage: In the heaven of Indra is hung a vast net of jewels, infinite in extent, and in each jewel are reflected all the others. So it is with all things: each contains every other, and each is contained in every other.

author: Mahayana synthesis
passage: There are two truths: conventional and ultimate. From the conventional standpoint, things appear as separate and substantial. From the ultimate standpoint, no thing has independent existence; only the dependent co-arising of all phenomena is real.

author: Ashtavakra
passage: You are the unfading, blissful, transcendent Self. Why do you wander in the cycle of birth and death? Liberation is your nature; nothing needs to be added or removed for you to be what you already are.

author: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
source: Brihadaranyaka, dialogue of Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi
passage: When there is duality, then one sees another, hears another, knows another. But when everything has become one's own Self, then by what should one see whom, hear whom, know whom?

author: Anonymous
passage: Make a cloud of forgetting between yourself and all things, and put a cloud of unknowing between yourself and God. Press into the darkness with a sharp dart of longing love. The mind cannot find Him; love can.

author: Jakob Boehme
source: synthesis of Boehme's writings on the divine ground
passage: The depth of the divine is in the depth of every soul. There is no place outside of God where God is not; what we call distance from God is only the soul's own forgetting of its own ground.

author: Junayd of Baghdad
passage: When the lover passes away from himself in the beloved, there is no lover and no beloved, only the One who was always both. This is fana — annihilation that is not destruction but the recognition of what was always so.

author: Mipham Rinpoche (and Dzogchen synthesis)
passage: The ground, path, and fruit of Dzogchen are not three things sequentially attained but one nature seen with increasing clarity. The fruit is what the ground always was; the path is the dissolving of the obscurations that prevent recognition.
